input.content:
Fortress revival · process review · 10 October 2026

Did the fixes of 8 October work?

On 8 October four changes to how the work runs landed together, just before batch 11. This page asks of each one: what was it for, and did it do that? Then it says what to fix next. Each part has a Select button, so that Speak can read it to you. The evidence at the foot of each part is left out of the selection.

Parts

  1. Words on this page
  2. The short answer
  3. The batch workflow
  4. The skill
  5. The record's new form
  6. The build speed-ups
  7. What cannot be told apart
  8. The reports and plain language
  9. Is the repository write-only?
  10. What to fix next
  11. Your waiting list

Words on this page

batch
Run of agents that makes four or five changes to Fortress together and lands them at once. Batches 8, 9 and 10 ran before the changes of 8 October. Batches 11, 12 and 13 ran after.
rung
One change to Fortress inside a batch, with the agents that make it and check it.
tokens written
Tokens an agent sends that are not read back from the cache. The project's cost unit. K means thousand and M means million.
skill
Text every agent loads first. Here it is the fortress-repo skill, which says how to work in this repository and what Fortress is.
record
Project's memory: FACTS, POSITIONS, PLAN, the gap ledger, INDEX and the notes.
gap ledger
List of every known gap in Fortress, one row each. Agents cite a row by its number.
relearning
Agent reading a script, or writing its own, to find out how to run something the project already knows how to run.
skeptic
Agent that checks a rung's change. Since batch 11 it also fixes what it finds.
judge
Agent that rules when a skeptic's fix may be disputed.

The short answer

  1. Met its aimThe batch workflow. Batches cost 15 % less, and a rung 27 % less. The costly second round of checking is gone. Quality did not drop, as far as six batches can show.
  2. Partly metThe skill. Agents stopped relearning what it explains. But it costs 0.47M to 0.65M tokens a batch, two to three times the plan. That is about ten times the relearning it removed. Its main job, giving agents a correct picture of Fortress, has never been measured.
  3. Partly metThe record's new form. It worked for the gap ledger, which shrank by more than half. FACTS is growing back. PLAN, where your questions go, never got the new form.
  4. Not measuredThe build speed-ups. Nobody measured the time after them. The one rough sign did not move.
  5. SmallThe reports' language. Sentences got shorter. But no report defines its terms, and the internal codes are as dense as before. What you read was already plain.
Evidence
  1. skill-effect.md lines 10, 56 to 59 and 80; the note's section 2.1.
  2. skill-effect.md lines 11, 46 and 79; the note's sections 2.2 and 3.
  3. record-growth/README.md lines 17 to 21; PLAN's size at each landing, the note's section 6.
  4. build-efficiency.md lines 11 to 23; the note's section 2.4.
  5. The note's section 3, from a prose count of every report of batches 8 to 13.

The note is explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/measures-judgement.md.

The batch workflow

Met its aim

What it was for. Before, a rung that its skeptic refused went to a judge, then a repair, then a second skeptic. That second round cost a fifth to a quarter of each batch. The redesign lets the skeptic fix what it finds, sends only a disputed fix to a judge, and drops the second skeptic. It also cut the briefs to a third or less. Batch 11 was forecast at about 5.2M tokens, against batch 10's 6.26M. You set the order of the work so that batch 11 would show a better shape than the wasteful runs before it.

What happened.

  1. Batches 8 to 10 wrote 7.7M, 6.9M and 6.3M tokens. Batches 11 to 13 wrote 5.0M, 5.4M and 7.2M. On average that is 15 % less.
  2. Per rung the fall is 27 %, from about 1.7M to about 1.3M.
  3. The second round of checking fell from 20 to 28 % of a batch to 3 to 6 %.
  4. Batch 11 came within 2 % of its forecast. Batch 13 cost 25 % more than its forecast. Most of the extra came from a machine restart that stopped two skeptics, and from one rung that measured something extra.
  5. Quality held, as far as the reviews can see. No wrong value landed. The review of the merged batch blocked nothing in batches 11 to 13. It had blocked one sentence in each of batches 8 and 9. Skeptics made 57 fixes, and all were sound. Six fixes went to a judge, and all six stood.
  6. Two costs grew. Each skeptic now writes about 400K, up from about 300K. And judges ruled six times on fixes that nobody disputed in substance, for 0.9M in all. You narrowed that rule on 9 October.

How sure. Sure that the saving comes from dropping the second round: those agents are gone, and their cost is on file. Less sure of its exact size, because the rungs differ from batch to batch. On quality, each batch has only one or two events to count, so "no loss" is all the evidence can say.

Evidence
  1. skill-effect.md lines 10 and 56 to 57.
  2. skill-effect.md line 59; means 1.74M and 1.26M, or 1.68M and 1.22M without the agents restarts killed.
  3. skill-effect.md line 80.
  4. batch-11-review.md lines 22 to 48; batch-13-review.md lines 36 to 55.
  5. skill-effect.md lines 90 to 104; batch-11-review.md line 227; batch-12-review.md line 232; batch-13-review.md line 259.
  6. skill-effect.md line 80; batch-13-review.md line 259; POSITIONS, "The judge's rulings." (POSITIONS.md line 118), commit a1902d0d4.

The aims: batch-redesign.md lines 12 to 16, 30 to 34 and 221; POSITIONS, "The order of the work after batch 10." (line 132).

The skill

Partly met

What it was for. Your position on the skills gives it four jobs. Gather what workers learned into one text for a reader new to the repository. Correct the wrong ideas about Fortress that agents bring from their training. Use short, plain sentences, close to Simplified Technical English, and never grow longer when rewritten. And the redesign gave it a fourth: carry the "how to" that left the briefs, for about 0.2M tokens a batch.

What happened.

  1. Agents stopped relearning what the skill explains. Reading scripts to learn how to run tests fell by 70 % for each agent. Two traps it warns about went from 28 cases to 2.
  2. Agents did not stop relearning what the skill leaves out. You decided that the two ladder measurements, the checker count and the distance, stay out of it. Reading their scripts fell only 17 % for each agent.
  3. One worker's discovery made the trip. A batch 10 worker found a debug flag by hand. It is now in the skill, and batch 13's workers used it 13 times.
  4. The saving from less relearning is small, about 0.4M a batch. This is counted in input-token equivalents, a unit that also counts text an agent keeps rereading.
  5. The skill costs far more. Every agent loads it. It costs 0.47M, 0.58M and 0.65M tokens written in batches 11 to 13, about a tenth of each batch. Counted in the same unit as the saving, it costs 4M to 5.4M a batch.
  6. Its sentences were already short before the rewrite: about 12 words on average, both before and after. The rewrite made the skill 9 % longer, not shorter. Its part on what the revival changed grows by about 7K characters a batch.
  7. Nobody has tested whether it gives agents a correct picture of Fortress.
  8. It brings a new risk: one wrong sentence reaches every agent. In batch 11, its command for long runs failed for every agent that used it. Each batch left 1 to 6 of its sentences false, for a writer to fix afterwards.

How sure. Sure of the cost. Fairly sure that the relearning fell because of the skill: in the same batches, what it covers fell sharply and what it leaves out barely moved. Nothing at all on its main job.

Evidence
  1. skill-effect.md line 79: 254 calls to 60 over 64 and 51 agents; traps 28 to 2.
  2. skill-effect.md line 79: stage driver reading 113 to 75, stage scripts 72 to 41; POSITIONS line 134 on the two measurements.
  3. context-study.md line 36; skill-effect.md line 79.
  4. skill-effect.md line 79: 0.59M, 0.49M, 0.67M against 0.19M, 0.17M, 0.17M.
  5. skill-effect.md lines 11 and 34 to 40; skill-load.py re-run on the three runs, totals equal; batch-redesign.md lines 68 and 210 for the plan.
  6. The note's sections 2.2 and 6: a prose count of the skill at commits 24af7743b^ and cae2a0ad5; part sizes from git ls-tree -r -l, 108.5K to 118.0K bytes without sources.md and the new part.
  7. reviews/fortress-pretraining-quiz.md and reviews/skills-distillation-audit.md section B exist; no run with the skill.
  8. batch-11-review.md lines 71 and 333 to 345; batch-12-review.md lines 296 to 311; batch-13-review.md lines 321 to 338.

The aims: POSITIONS, "The skills are written for a reader new to the repository, and checked against what the workers did." (POSITIONS.md line 134).

The record's new form

Partly met

What it was for. Your words: "I don't want you to be searching with a flashlight in a dark room. I want to give you a map of the territory." So FACTS and POSITIONS say only what is true now, and the history goes to separate files. FACTS is cleaned up before each batch, since workers pay to read it.

One correction to the dates. You decided this form on 30 September, and FACTS got it then and on 2 October. On 8 October only the gap ledger got it.

What happened.

  1. The gap ledger shrank from 1.25M to 0.54M characters. It now grows about 19K a batch, where it grew 46K before.
  2. FACTS fell to 227K characters on 2 October. It has grown back to 294K. The last two clean-ups changed it by almost nothing.
  3. Each landing makes some FACTS sentences false: 4, 6 and 10 in batches 11 to 13. They are fixed after.
  4. Workers read less of the record through the slice chosen for them. But the slices were cut in the same hour, so the form cannot take the credit.
  5. Mistakes from the record did not fall. A premise of the record that was wrong: 13 cases before, 10 after. The record claiming more than the code does: 15 cases before, 17 after.
  6. PLAN never got the new form. It holds your questions, answered items, and one list per batch for your review. It grew from 330K to 464K characters in three batches.

How sure. Sure for the ledger, whose sizes are exact. There is no evidence either way that the map prevents mistakes.

Evidence
  1. record-growth/README.md lines 17 to 19.
  2. record-growth/README.md line 21; FACTS at each landing, the note's section 6.
  3. batch-11-review.md line 364; batch-12-review.md line 85; batch-13-review.md line 107.
  4. skill-effect.md lines 67 and 76; batch-redesign.md line 66.
  5. skill-effect.md lines 99, 100 and 115.
  6. git show of PLAN at the base of batch 11 and at each landing: 329,694, 346,564, 389,197, 442,362, and 464,142 now.

The aims: POSITIONS, "The record's form: an optimized build and a debug build." (line 130) and "The gap ledger's form." (line 133). The date: POSITIONS-history.md lines 448 to 452; the ledger rewrite is commit ae4f8e38a.

The build speed-ups

Not measured

What it was for. Builds and test runs that keep their caches. A build with nothing changed went from 20 seconds to 4. A one-test run with a warm cache takes about 3 seconds instead of 18. Before, 120 test runs in batches 8 to 10 started with an empty cache, about 4 hours of waiting. The aim was time, not tokens.

What happened.

  1. No tool measured the time after it. The script that measured it before was lost with its author's transcript.
  2. One rough sign: a one-test run took about 34 seconds a call before, and 31 after. That is no real change. But agents now start long runs in the background, so this sign is weak.
  3. The build counts in the study are wrong. The counting tool counts refused builds and misses background builds. The reviews counted by hand: every build in batches 11 and 12 was on new code.
  4. The test suites now run on four threads, and passed in all three gates.

How sure. Not measured either way.

Evidence
  1. tools/transcript-study/README.md line 29.
  2. The study's cost.py output over batches 8 to 13: rung workers' one-test runs 87 calls in 50 minutes, then 62 calls in 32 minutes.
  3. batch-11-review.md lines 68 to 70; batch-12-review.md line 73; batch-10-review.md line 392.
  4. batch-11-review.md line 79; batch-13-review.md line 105.

The aims: build-efficiency.md lines 11 to 23; harness-cache-cost.md line 13.

What cannot be told apart

Some causes landed together, so the evidence cannot say which one did what.

  1. The new workflow and the skill landed in the same hour. No batch had one without the other.
  2. There was no "old skill". Batches 8 to 10 had no skill at all. Their briefs carried the procedures.
  3. The ledger rewrite and the shorter briefings came the same day as the skill.
  4. The work itself differs from batch to batch.
  5. Machine restarts made agents run twice in batches 9 and 13.
  6. The skill was corrected after each batch, so each batch ran on a different version.
  7. The counts are small: one or two events per batch.
Evidence
  1. skill-effect.md lines 119 to 120.
  2. skill-effect.md line 9.
  3. Commits ae4f8e38a, 24af7743b to cae2a0ad5, e02015985, all on 8 October.
  4. skill-effect.md line 121.
  5. skill-effect.md line 122.
  6. Commits 7b3226bb2, 38def33a9, 6c021c983.
  7. skill-effect.md section 5.

The reports and plain language

Small

Your reading. The batch reports now follow the skill's form and voice, define their terms first, and read as plain language instead of agent shorthand.

What was measured. The prose of every report of batches 8 to 13, without code, tables and headings.

  1. Sentences got shorter. A rung report's average sentence went from 21 words to 18. Sentences over 30 words went from about 1 in 5 to about 1 in 9.
  2. Reports got shorter, from 5.3K words to 3.9K.
  3. Internal codes did not drop. Codes such as "row 582", "item 43", "Q4" and commit codes come about 1.3 times per 100 words, before and after. These are what make a report hard to follow without the record.
  4. No report defines its terms. Not one of 26 rung reports, 6 batch records or 6 reviews.
  5. The batch record that the gathering agent writes got denser. Its typical sentence went from 16 words to 24.
  6. What reaches you was already plain. The "For Pavol" part of each review had sentences of 12 to 14 words in batch 8, as in batch 13.
  7. The study notes that open with their terms started on 5 October, from the coordinator's briefs, before the rewrite.
  8. The old brief told workers to write plain sentences. The new brief does not, and neither does the skill. So the shorter sentences came from what the agents read: the skill, or the shorter briefs. Those two cannot be told apart.

Against the cost. The change is real but small. It does not give you reports you can read. It does not change the balance either: the skill costs about ten times the relearning it saves. Its case rests on a claim nobody has tested, that it prevents wrong changes. That can be tested cheaply, and its cost can be cut. See points 2 and 5 of "What to fix next".

Evidence
  1. The note's section 3: means over 12 and 14 reports, 21.3 to 17.7 words; over 30 words 20.9 % to 11.2 %.
  2. The same count: 5,332 and 3,883 words a report on average.
  3. The same count: 1.34 and 1.29 codes per 100 words.
  4. No terms section and no definition list in any of them.
  5. Median sentence 16 to 24 words; over 30 words 22 % to 35 %.
  6. "For Pavol" sections of batch-8-review.md to batch-13-review.md.
  7. checking-roles-cost.md, context-study.md, testing-practices.md, harness-cache-cost.md, all before the rewrite; skill-effect.md, written after, is the densest at 27.5 words a sentence.
  8. The old brief, climb-batch-workflow.js at 9c9e823d5, lines 1020 to 1022; the new one at 83b1cae78, lines 576 to 604 and 686.

Is the repository write-only?

What a batch writes. Each batch writes 25K to 54K words of reports, plus a review of 7K to 9K words. Read aloud, that is three to six hours a batch. The record holds 1,655 files and 38M characters. FACTS, PLAN, the ledger and INDEX grew by 45K to 95K characters a batch.

What workers still learn on their own.

  1. What the skill covers, hardly at all now.
  2. The two ladder measurements, still. In batch 13, one worker ran one of them in the foreground for 10 minutes, because its brief said it takes 20 seconds. That cost a 309K-token reload of the worker's memory.
  3. Whether workers rediscover facts already on record was measured only for batch 10. It was 4 % of their cost.

What they read from the record.

  1. A slice chosen for each rung: about 4 % of a batch.
  2. Record files they open themselves: about 4 to 5 %.
  3. The reports of their own rung: 7 to 8 %.
  4. The skill's part on what the revival changed: 13 of 14 workers read it. It is the one distilled record that reaches them.
  5. They do not use INDEX.

Did mistakes from the record fall?

  1. No. And the skill added a new kind: false sentences in the skill itself.

Your side.

  1. Nothing sums up the work for you except the short "For Pavol" part of each review.
  2. Batches hand you 22 to 53 items each. Of the 47 items of batch 13 that reached PLAN, 46 already had a default that landed, or were for information. Only one needed your word.
  3. PLAN's lists for your review now hold 202 entries, and answered items stay listed as open.

Has the summing up paid off? For workers, partly. The skill carries the how-to and the revival's changes to every agent, and they stopped relearning what it covers. For you, no. Nothing in the record is made for you to read, and your list grows by tens of items a batch.

How each reader should go through the record

For you, in this order:

  1. The "For Pavol" part of each batch review. It is under 400 words.
  2. One short list of what needs your word: items with no default, steps that cannot be undone, and changes against one of your decisions.
  3. When you want to know what Fortress is now: the skill's "Fortress as a language", and its part on what the revival changed. It is kept current and checked after every batch.
  4. A report only when an item in your list points you to one section of it.

For a worker, in this order:

  1. Its brief.
  2. The skill's main page, then the parts for its area.
  3. Its slice of the record.
  4. The ledger rows it needs, found by search.
  5. The code, the library and the specification.
  6. A report only when a fact or a ledger row points to it. Never INDEX.
Evidence
  1. skill-effect.md line 79.
  2. batch-13-review.md line 98.
  3. context-study.md line 33.
  4. skill-effect.md line 67.
  5. skill-effect.md line 76.
  6. skill-effect.md line 68.
  7. skill-load.py re-run on batches 11 to 13: 29 reads by rung workers; 105 of the part's 138 reads are by the agents that maintain it.
  8. context-study.md lines 23 and 34.
  9. skill-effect.md lines 99, 100 and 115; the reviews' parts on false skill sentences.
  10. The "For Pavol" sections, 240 to 384 words.
  11. batch-11-review.md lines 315 to 323; batch-12-review.md line 317; batch-13-review.md lines 344 to 351.
  12. PLAN.md, the "listed for his review" sections; batch-11-review.md line 362; batch-13-review.md lines 380 to 387.

The word counts and sizes: the note's sections 4 and 6.

What to fix next

Each item says why first, then what it would save and cost, then how a later review would measure it. The recommendation comes last. A rung costs about 1.2M tokens across its agents, for scale.

1. A short list for you

Batches hand you tens of items, and almost all of them need nothing from you. PLAN keeps every one, and grows by up to 53K characters a batch. Answered items stay listed as open. If the items whose default has landed moved to a history file, as FACTS' history does, your list would hold a handful a batch. Sorting the 202 entries once costs about 0.4M tokens, a third of a rung. After that it costs under 0.02M a batch. A later review would count the items in your list each batch, and track PLAN's size with the record-growth script.

Recommendation. Give PLAN the same two-file form as FACTS: a short list of what needs your word, and a history of the rest.

2. Cheaper reading of the skill

Every agent reads the same skill text and pays to load it: 0.47M to 0.65M a batch. A test on this machine showed that text placed in a project agent type is loaded once. The next agents read it from the cache, at a tenth of the price. That would save about 0.35M to 0.5M a batch, 6 to 8 %. First a probe of about 0.1M must show whether a changed agent type is picked up without restarting the session. If it is not, only the parts that rarely change go in. A later review would see the saving in the first-call figures of the batch measures script, and in the skill-load script.

Recommendation. Run the probe, and if it passes, serve the skill's standing text through one agent type.

3. Keep the skill true

Each batch left 1 to 6 skill sentences false. One false sentence made every agent of batch 11 fail its first long command. Today a writer fixes them after the review. A worker already lists the specification sentences its change makes false. It could list skill sentences the same way, and the gathering agent could fix them before the landing. That costs about 0.03M a batch. A later review counts the false sentences left, and the goal is none.

Recommendation. Add skill sentences to what a worker's report lists, and fix them before the landing.

4. Say how to run the two ladder measurements

You decided that the skill leaves these two out, and that the briefs say how to run them. The briefs do not say enough: workers still read the scripts and write their own. One worker's 10-minute wait cost 309K tokens. A paragraph of about 1K tokens in the right briefs would cover it, about 0.01M a batch. It would save about 0.3M a batch in input-token equivalents, plus the odd reload. The recovered testing-practices scripts count it.

Recommendation. Add one paragraph on running the ladder measurements to the briefs of the roles that run them.

5. Test the skill's main job directly

The skill's main job is to correct wrong ideas about Fortress, and nobody has measured that. The study proposed a test inside a batch: two rungs, one with the skill and one without. With one pair, and one or two events a batch, it cannot show a difference, and it costs a rung or more. A quiz already exists. A fresh agent wrote what it believes about Fortress, and a reviewer graded every claim. Running it again with the skill's main page in hand would count the wrong claims the skill corrects. It costs about 0.15M.

Recommendation. Skip the test inside a batch, and run the Fortress quiz again, with and without the skill.

6. Fix the build count

The tool that counts builds counts refused builds, and misses builds started in the background. Two reviews asked for a fix, and it is still not done. It costs about 0.05M. It is fixed when its count matches the reviews' hand counts, 11 and 13.

Recommendation. Fix the build count in the batch measures script.

7. Measure the build speed-ups once

Nothing measured the time the build work saved. The earlier count can be rebuilt from the recovered scripts: a first test that takes over 10 seconds started with an empty cache. It costs about 0.15M on Sonnet, since it is counting, not judgement.

Recommendation. Count the empty-cache test runs of batches 11 to 14 once.

8. Already done: the judge rule
